name: G.11

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York

support: Stake or trellis for life; crops come early and heavy
soil_notes: fertile, well-drained ground with irrigation in dry spells; copes with replant soils better than M.9/M.26
best_for: high-density spindle or trellis orchards and small gardens wanting an M.9-sized tree with fire-blight insurance
avoid_when: woolly-aphid-prone warm regions without aphid control; dry unirrigated or grassed sites; winters colder than zone 5 until its hardiness is better proven
variety_fit: Cornell suggests it for strong-growing varieties; weak growers such as Honeycrisp can stay too small on it.
notes: Tree size matches M.9 T337 or runs slightly larger, with yield efficiency at or above M.9 and good fruit size; it was among the most efficient moderate dwarfs in the 8-year 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial. Moderately resistant to fire blight (rarely killed through the rootstock, but not immune) and to crown rot, and tolerant of replant soils, but woolly apple aphid colonises its roots. Roots well in stoolbeds, which made it one of the easiest Geneva stocks to obtain.

name: G.16

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: US plant patent PP12,443 (2002); now planted far less than G.41 or G.11.

support: Root system anchors well, but a stake or trellis is needed to carry the crop
soil_notes: needs fertile, well-drained, weed-free soil like M.9; irrigate in dry spells
best_for: M.9-sized trees in fire-blight regions when certified virus-free scions are available
avoid_when: scionwood of unknown virus status (e.g. grafting from old heritage trees); woolly-aphid-prone regions
variety_fit: Use only virus-tested budwood; unsuitable for top-working or home grafting from old trees that may carry latent viruses.
notes: A full dwarf about the size of M.9 that crops very early, is nearly immune to fire blight, tolerates collar rot and makes almost no suckers or burr knots. Its serious flaw is hypersensitivity to common latent viruses: trees budded with infected wood can decline or die, so certified virus-free scions are essential. Susceptible to woolly apple aphid; it was among the best survivors of the 2004-05 New York cold snap.

name: G.30

origin.place: Cornell University apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Released by Cornell in the 1990s; tested in the 1994 NC-140 semi-dwarf trial.

support: Stake or trellis at least for the first years; the union can snap under early crops or wind
soil_notes: broadly adaptable; tolerates heavier, wetter soils better than MM.106 thanks to crown-rot tolerance
best_for: semi-dwarf orchard or garden trees in fire-blight country where an M.7-sized tree should crop much sooner
avoid_when: unsupported trees on windy sites; brittle-union varieties; woolly-aphid-prone regions
variety_fit: Union strength varies widely by scion: in Cornell nursery tests Northern Spy, Fuji and Golden Delicious made strong unions while Wijcik McIntosh, James Grieve and Cox were among the weakest.
notes: A semi-dwarf usually placed near M.7 in size (reports range from M.26 to M.7 depending on site) but far earlier-bearing and more productive than M.7. Highly resistant to fire blight and tolerant of crown rot, with few suckers and rare burr knots, and it came through the 2004-05 New York freezes well. The graft union is brittle with some varieties, so young trees need support, and woolly apple aphid can infest the roots.

name: G.41

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Released 2005; sold as stoolbed (N) and tissue-culture (TC) liners.

support: Trellis or permanent stake; brittle union with some varieties
soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil with irrigation; small root system like M.9, but copes well with replant ground
best_for: high-density trellis orchards, cordons and espaliers, especially on replant sites or where fire blight and woolly aphid are problems
avoid_when: free-standing trees without support; windy exposed sites; dry, poor or grassed ground
variety_fit: Cornell recommends it for weak-growing varieties and replant sites; with brittle-union scions such as Honeycrisp or Envy (Scilate) support the union from planting.
notes: An M.9-sized dwarf with very high yield efficiency and strong resistance to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, plus good replant tolerance - the nearest thing to a disease-proof M.9. It is very cold hardy (good survival in the 2004-05 New York freezes) and also does well in warm climates such as Mexico. Drawbacks are poor rooting in stoolbeds (hence tissue-culture liners, which gave slightly smaller trees in NC-140 trials) and a brittle graft union with some cultivars.

name: G.202

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Released for New Zealand in 2002 and for the US in 2004.

soil_notes: reasonably fertile, well-drained soil; tolerant of replant ground
best_for: M.26-sized trees where woolly apple aphid and fire blight are both problems (warm temperate regions, replant sites)
avoid_when: unsupported trees on exposed sites; very cold-winter zones where its hardiness is unproven
variety_fit: A good match for weak growers such as Honeycrisp; Cornell pairs it with G.935 for very weak varieties.
notes: About M.26 in size, precocious and productive, with resistance to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid plus replant tolerance; aphid resistance made it the first Geneva choice for New Zealand. Stoolbed-grown liners gave noticeably larger trees than tissue-culture liners in the 2010 NC-140 trial, and it suckered more than M.26 there. Stoolbed rooting is moderate and its winter hardiness is less documented than that of G.41 or G.935.

name: G.210

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Cornell / USDA-ARS), Geneva, New York

support: Stake or trellis in high-density plantings; early reports questioned its anchorage
soil_notes: adapts to average and lighter soils; vigorous enough for weaker ground and replant sites
best_for: organic orchards, weaker soils and semi-dwarf garden trees that should still crop early
avoid_when: where a small tree is wanted; severe-winter zones until hardiness is better documented
variety_fit: Suits weak-growing varieties that would stall on a dwarf; strong varieties may grow too large for close spacing.
notes: Semi-dwarf in the M.7 class (some trials place it between M.7 and MM.106) but precocious and at least as yield-efficient as M.9. Resistant to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, tolerant of replant disease, and roots well in stoolbeds. Cornell positions it mainly for organic production, poorer soils and weak scions.

name: G.214

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: US plant patent PP23,516; trialled as CG.4214 in the 2010 NC-140 trial.

soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil with irrigation; dense fibrous roots explore soil well for a dwarf
best_for: high-density trellis orchards wanting M.9 Pajam 2 vigour with full fire blight and woolly aphid resistance
avoid_when: unsupported trees; poor dry ground; severe-winter zones until hardiness is better documented
variety_fit: Performs well with Honeycrisp and Fuji in trials; vigour suits most commercial varieties at close spacing.
notes: A dwarf close to M.9 Pajam 2 in vigour with very high yield efficiency; as CG.4214 it was among the most efficient large dwarfs over 8 years in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial. Resistant to fire blight and crown rot, immune to woolly apple aphid, replant tolerant and with a dense, finely branched root system. Propagates easily in stoolbeds; cold hardiness is less documented than for G.41 or G.935.

name: G.222

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York

soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil with irrigation, as for other dwarfs
best_for: high-density orchards needing a dwarf with fire blight, crown rot and woolly aphid resistance
avoid_when: unsupported trees; poor dry ground; cold-winter zones until hardiness data accumulate
notes: A newer dwarf from the same M.27 x Robusta 5 family as G.41 and G.202, sized between M.9 Pajam 2 and M.26 (Cornell's 2024 chart groups it with M.26). It bears as early as M.9 and was more yield-efficient than M.9 and M.26 in Cornell trials, resists fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, and shows some replant tolerance. Its commercial track record is still short.
